item.title: Ago Bay: Pearl Rafts and Island-Dotted Waters — Guide
item.description: Ago Bay is the scenic heart of the Ise-Shima region, a deeply indented ria coastline where the sea reaches inland among dozens of forested islets and countless rafts of cultivated pearl oysters, forming one of Japan’s most beautiful and productive stretches of water. This is the cradle of the pearl industry Mikimoto founded, and the classic way to appreciate it is from the water — sightseeing boats, some styled as Spanish galleons, and glass-bottom cruises glide among the islands and pearl rafts, revealing the oyster culture below.

item.title: Ama Divers and Their Seafood Huts: Ise-Shima's Living Tradition — Guide
item.description: The ama are the traditional women free-divers of Ise-Shima, who for perhaps 3,000 years have plunged into the coastal waters without tanks or air, holding their breath to gather abalone, turban shells, sea urchin and seaweed — a physically astonishing craft passed down through generations of women, some still diving into their eighties. Today many ama welcome visitors into their amagoya, the huts where they once warmed themselves between dives, to grill the day’s catch — abalone, scallops, spiny lobster and turban shells — over a charcoal hearth while sharing stories of a fast-vanishing way of life.

item.title: Tekone Sushi: Ise-Shima's Fisherman's Bowl — Guide
item.description: Tekone-zushi is the beloved fisherman’s dish of the Ise-Shima coast, born of practicality on the katsuo (bonito) boats: fishermen would slice their fresh catch, marinate it quickly in soy sauce, and mix it by hand into vinegared rice to eat between hauls — ‘tekone’ meaning ‘hand-mixed’. Today it is a regional specialty served in restaurants around Ise, Toba and Shima: glossy slices of soy-marinated bonito (or tuna) fanned over sushi rice, scattered with shiso, ginger and sesame, its rich, savoury simplicity a delicious counterpoint to the refined seafood kaiseki of the coast.
